item.title: Artspace Guåhan to open ‘You Are Here’ exhibition
item.description: Artspace Guåhasn will open its new exhibition, You Are Here, on Oct. 15, at its studio in Tamuning. The exhibition brings together different artistic perspectives and explores how personal histories, identities, experiences, and surroundings can influence how people understand themselves and the world around them.
item.content:encoded:
Artspace Guåhasn will open its new exhibition, You Are Here, on Oct. 15, at its studio in Tamuning.

The exhibition brings together different artistic perspectives and explores how personal histories, identities, experiences, and surroundings can influence how people understand themselves and the world around them.

The exhibition centers on the question, “What does HERE mean to YOU?” and invites visitors to consider their own connections to place and belonging through the artwork on display.

Artspace Guåhan will bring together artists with different perspectives and ask visitors to consider what being “ here ” means to them. Deane Jessee-Jones, secretary of the board of directors, says the exhibition supports local artists of varying ages.

She said, “We do not collect any commission… all of the profits go directly to the artist.”

Artspace Guåhan is a Guam-based nonprofit that works to make art accessible and provide opportunities for local artists to exhibit and connect with the community.

The opening runs from 6 to 7:30 p.m. and will include an opportunity to meet the artists.

The exhibition will remain on display through Dec. 3.

You Are Here is free and open to the public.

item.title: U.S. Supreme Court hears arguments in Andersen open detonation case
item.description: The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments on Wednesday, Washington, D.C. time, in a case involving an open detonation pit on Andersen Air Force Base. The group Prutehi Guåhan sued the Air Force in 2022, arguing that open detonation of hazardous waste and unexploded ordnance endangers Guam’s environment, cultural heritage and ancestral lands.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments on Wednesday, Washington, D.C. time, in a case involving an open detonation pit on Andersen Air Force Base.

The group Prutehi Guåhan sued the Air Force in 2022, arguing that open detonation of hazardous waste and unexploded ordnance endangers Guam’s environment, cultural heritage and ancestral lands.

In May 2021, the Air Force applied for a three-year renewal of its hazardous waste facility permit with the Guam Environmental Protection Agency. In court filings, Prutehi Guåhan stated that the Air Force failed to conduct an environmental assessment of its actions as required by the National Environmental Policy Act.

The case was dismissed in the District Court of Guam, but the 9 th Circuit Court of Appeals sided with Prutehi Guåhan and reinstated the case.

The Supreme Court is considering whether the Air Force’s request to renew its permit would be a “final agency action” that can be reviewed by the courts. Justices are also considering whether federal agencies must comply with NEPA requirements before seeking to renew environmental permits.

During oral arguments before the court, Department of Justice attorney Sopan Joshi argued that filing a permit application is not a final agency action.

“It’s a request to someone else to take action,” he said. “Filing a permit application triggers a back-and-forth process whose outcome is, by definition, a moving target until a decision on the permit is issued. Treating an application as final would just lead to a multiplicity of suits throughout a permitting process, which I think defeats the whole point of the finality requirement.”

Chief Justice John Roberts, a George W. Bush appointee, asked Joshi when the Air Force’s decision to operate the detonation pit would be considered final.

“So are you saying that there’s no point at which the Air Force’s decision can be challenged?” he asked. “The Air Force’s action is never final and, therefore, never reviewable?”

“The application is never going to become final agency action,” Joshi said. “And there is no cause of action under NEPA itself. Congress didn't provide one. So any review would have to go through the [Administrative Procedure Act], and I don't think the APA provides a cause of action for this application at any point in time.”

Earthjustice attorney Caroline Flynn, representing Prutehi Guåhan, said the Air Force’s final action is clear.

“We know that the Air Force is settled on that decision because it has, in fact, been acting on them past -- you know, by continuing these detonation operations past September 2021, when they otherwise would have ceased.”

The justices will consider the arguments, and a ruling will likely take several months.

item.title: ‘Struggling to keep this government going’: Apatang warns of furloughs, rising austerity after signing strained CNMI budget
item.description: The CNMI is facing deep fiscal strain as Gov. David M. Apatang defended his line‑item vetoes in the newly signed fiscal 2027 budget, which is built on $100.7 million in projected General Fund revenues. Apatang signed the budget Tuesday night, ending a five‑day partial shutdown that left non‑essential employees without pay.
item.content:encoded:
The CNMI is facing deep fiscal strain as Gov. David M. Apatang defended his line‑item vetoes in the newly signed fiscal 2027 budget, which is built on $100.7 million in projected General Fund revenues.

Apatang signed the budget Tuesday night, ending a five‑day partial shutdown that left non‑essential employees without pay.

Apatang said he vetoed several provisions he deemed unconstitutional or financially impossible, including a mandate requiring the administration to “front‑load” $16 million to the Public School System. He said the CNMI cannot afford the upfront payment and must instead fund PSS monthly. The Senate’s final budget version allocates $25 million for PSS—down from the $32 million proposed by both the governor and the House.

“It breaks my heart to reduce PSS funding,” Apatang said, adding that a three‑day school week would be unacceptable but may be unavoidable unless the PSS board finds operational efficiencies.

The governor said the administration is “scraping the bottom of the barrel,” warning that furloughs—estimated at up to 400 employees—may be necessary once Civil Service Commission regulations are finalized. He also confirmed retirees will lose their 25% government contribution after Oct. 15, though he is searching for funds to soften the impact.

Apatang defended his administration against criticism over the CNMI’s fiscal collapse, saying he inherited years of unresolved audit findings and depleted federal relief funds.

“I didn’t spend all this money,” he said. “We’re struggling to keep this government going.”

He urged agencies to tighten operations, reduce expenses, and avoid unnecessary vehicle use. He also asked Commonwealth Public Utilities Corp. to reconsider CUC’s proposed rate increase, calling it “a drastic burden” residents cannot afford.

On tourism and economic recovery, Apatang said federal immigration and travel policies continue to hinder the CNMI’s ability to rebuild air service and visitor arrivals. He said he has repeatedly asked federal officials to visit the Commonwealth and understand its strategic importance.

With three months left in his term, Apatang said the next administration will face a difficult road.

“Good luck,” he said. “I’ll pray for you. It’s going to be a tough one.”

item.title: Attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and wounded over 300 more, Saudi authorities say

item.content:encoded:
CAIRO (AP) — The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia's capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured over 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early Sunday, with some in critical condition.

The attack was the deadliest in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war, whose fronts have expanded to include the recent surge in fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi-backed government forces there.

The statement, which did not assign blame for the attack, said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.

The attack — the latest of several in the past week on King Khalid International Airport that killed four people — is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies including the United States to provide military support for the kingdom.

Shortly after the attack on Saturday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis. "We may. We're going to look at it," Trump said. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."

A missile struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media.

The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis. There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital. The rebels at times take days to claim responsibility.

Riyadh airport operations were suspended

Saudi civil aviation authorities earlier said airport operations were suspended. An official notice to aviators said the suspension was through midnight. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed.

Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport. Statements later turned to condolences.

Later on Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition said a projectile had fallen near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and a Houthi-launched ballistic missile had been intercepted in Al-Kharj governorate, southeast of Riyadh.

The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.

Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along Yemen's Red Sea coast. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.

Though the Houthis have told the AP and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that.

Saudi Arabia has run low on interceptors, officials say

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.

Officials have said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive against the Houthis.

Earlier Saturday, Saudi Arabia said its foreign minister and Omani counterpart spoke by phone about the importance of "supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions" in the region. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region.

The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.

Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis' ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a "greater focus on aviation infrastructure."

The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts "create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft," it said.

Two regional officials said Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport on Thursday damaged three planes. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to brief the media. The Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board.

Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that "filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability."

Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington and Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut contributed to this report.

item.title: The Kennedy Center names new artistic director, amid concerns
item.description: The Kennedy Center has named Rick Canny, a talent manager who has worked with acts including ZZ Top and former Mötley Crüe drummer Tommy Lee, as its new artistic director. His appointment came despite complaints from staff about his business practices as a consultant for the arts institution. item.content:encoded:
The Kennedy Center has named Rick Canny, a talent manager who has worked with acts including ZZ Top and former Mötley Crüe drummer Tommy Lee, as its new artistic director. His appointment came despite complaints from staff about his business practices as a consultant for the arts institution.

According to an email obtained by NPR sent to high-level staff Thursday, Matt Floca, the center's executive director and chief operating officer, announced that Canny would be the center's new artistic director. Canny has served as a consultant to the Kennedy Center since shortly after President Trump became the institution's chairman in February 2025.

Floca has no background in arts administration, programming or fundraising, in contrast to chief administrators at similar performing arts venues around the country. He was previously head of facilities at the Kennedy Center before being promoted in March , and holds a degree in construction management.

Floca wrote: "Rick will advise me and the broader leadership team on artistic strategy, business practices, presenting and talent curation, ticketing and pricing models, media opportunities, and programming sponsorships."

Floca also wrote: "Since April 2025, Rick has worked with the Center as a consultant through his firm, Favor the Artist, including serving as creative lead for the Kennedy Center Honors and the Mark Twain Prize. He will continue in this capacity while serving as the Center's Artistic Director."

The Kennedy Center is mostly closed, but it says it will maintain a small amount of public and educational programming, while the entire closure is being contested in federal court. The previous head of programming came and left within two weeks in January .

Arts administrators around the country have told NPR that booking performances for performing arts centers is done years in advance.

The Kennedy Center did not respond to NPR's requests for comment on Canny's appointment, but confirmed the contents of the email. Canny also did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Favor the Artist 's website does not include any information about its client roster or about the firm's history. The published lists of his professional background indicate that Canny has little experience in programming the kinds of performers more typically booked at a venue such as the Kennedy Center, including marquee contemporary solo performers and groups, orchestras, and dance and theater troupes.

NPR has obtained an internal memo written in March by the center's then-senior director of music programming, Sammy Miller, raising concerns about fees and expenses charged by Canny. NPR has reached out to Miller for comment, but did not receive a reply.

In that memo, sent to Floca and the Kennedy Center's human resources department, Miller said that during one month in early 2026, Canny had charged the center $30,000 in consulting fees. And in another month, Canny had charged over $28,000 in fees and travel expenses, including two first-class round-trip flights between Los Angeles and Washington, D.C.

The Kennedy Center did not reply to NPR's request for comment regarding staff concerns about Canny. In a statement to The New York Times on Friday, the center said that the $30,000 fee "did not reflect Mr. Canny's current agreement," but did not provide specifics. The institution also told the Times that Canny's travel expenses had been reviewed.

Miller wrote that he had previously tried to resolve his concerns through the center's general counsel and its finance office, but "both offices appear to be protecting Mr. Canny."

In its recent public statements and court filings, the Kennedy Center has repeatedly claimed to be on the verge of bankruptcy . Last month, Trump said that the arts institution has lost "hundreds of millions" of dollars. Trump has not offered evidence to support that claim.

The Kennedy Center remains shut to the public while Trump and the center's board, most of whom were hand-selected by the president, fight in a federal court to shutter the institution for two years for a large-scale renovation. Last month, Trump threatened to tear down the center if his name is not prominently displayed on the building.

item.title: At least 2 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama
item.description: Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are surveying damage wrought by Hurricane Isaias, after the storm bashed into the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm Friday night. At least two people have died from storm-related incidents, NPR has confirmed. Isaias brought 105 mph winds onshore, snapping trees and knocking out electricity. Officials warn that flash flood threats persist, but further inland.
item.content:encoded:
Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are surveying damage wrought by Hurricane Isaias, after the storm bashed into the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm Friday night. At least two people have died from storm-related incidents, NPR has confirmed.

Isaias brought 105 mph winds onshore, snapping trees and knocking out electricity. Officials warn that flash flood threats persist, but further inland.

One death occurred in Escambia County, in the far west of the Florida Panhandle. Shortly before 9 p.m. local time Friday, a rescue team found a person pinned under a large tree, according to Sgt. Melony Peterson of the Escambia County Sheriff's Office.

"The victim was inside the home when the tree collapsed," Peterson said via email.

Another death was reported in Jefferson County, Ala., which includes Birmingham.

"We did have a storm-related fatality overnight," Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency Director Jim Coker told NPR. "A tree did fall on the house," Coker added. "It was a single-family residence."

As of 11:50 a.m. ET Saturday, about 780,000 power customers remained without power in Florida, Alabama and Georgia, according to the monitoring site Poweroutage.us . That figure had been closer to 900,000 earlier Saturday.

In Florida, the worst outages were in counties such as Santa Rosa; Holmes; Washington; and Walton – all of which had more than 80% of their residents without power, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a morning news conference.

The governor said some 16,000 utility workers were busy trying to get power returned to homeowners.

"Last night in the wee hours of the morning, those crews began working as early as 3 a.m.," DeSantis said. He added that teams were also working to remove trees blocking main roads -- and that both I-10 and Route 98 were open as of Saturday morning, along with all state bridges.

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane around 8:30 p.m. local time Friday night, packing 105 mph winds, according to the National Hurricane Center . It brought a storm surge of some 5 feet -- short of the 6 to 9 feet forecasters had said was possible if landfall coincided with peak high tide. It arrived roughly two hours before high tide in Destin.

Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical storm hours after making landfall. By 5 a.m. local time on Saturday, its sustained winds had dropped to 35 mph, as the system sped its way through Alabama.

"Multiple trees and power lines are down across the county," tweeted the emergency management agency in Jefferson County, Ala. It told residents to "avoid unnecessary travel if possible while crews clear roads and restore service."

But the storm's effects extended for hundreds of miles. By around 9:30 a.m. Saturday, the system sent a long band of powerful thunder storms up the center of Georgia. And as the Florida Public Radio Emergency Network notes, forecasters warn that tornadoes could spin off of the system, causing further havoc far from the Gulf Coast.
